reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AABB Technical Manual
clinicalPearls: The most common inherited thrombophilia in people of European ancestry, arising from a single point mutation in the factor V gene
The mutated factor Va resists inactivation by activated protein C, so thrombin generation continues unchecked
Heterozygotes have a modestly increased risk of venous thromboembolism, while homozygotes carry a substantially higher risk
Risk rises markedly when the variant is combined with other factors such as oestrogen use, pregnancy, surgery, or immobility
It predisposes mainly to venous rather than arterial thrombosis and is associated with some pregnancy complications
Screening begins with a functional activated protein C resistance assay, confirmed by genetic testing for the specific mutation
A positive result seldom alters the intensity or standard duration of anticoagulation after a first provoked event, so testing should be reserved for situations where it will change management
reference.pathophysiology: Factor V Leiden results from a guanine-to-adenine substitution that changes an arginine residue at a cleavage site in factor V. Activated protein C normally inactivates factor Va at this site to dampen coagulation; the mutation removes this cleavage site, so factor Va persists and continues to support thrombin generation. This state of activated protein C resistance shifts haemostasis toward clot formation. Because the defect is a gain of prothrombotic function rather than loss of an anticoagulant protein, its per-copy thrombotic risk is lower than for antithrombin, protein C, or protein S deficiency, but its high population frequency makes it the commonest inherited contributor to venous thrombosis.
additionalDifferentials: Protein C or protein S deficiency
Acquired activated protein C resistance from pregnancy or oestrogen therapy
additionalInvestigations: Functional activated protein C resistance assay as an initial screen
Genetic testing confirming the factor V Leiden mutation and zygosity
Assessment for coexisting thrombophilias where clinically relevant
Evaluation of provoking factors surrounding any thrombotic event
Family history review and selective counselling before relative testing
redFlags: Venous thromboembolism, especially extensive or at an unusual site, in a homozygous individual
Thrombosis provoked by oestrogen therapy or pregnancy in a known carrier
Recurrent events despite anticoagulation, prompting reassessment
Combined thrombophilic defects amplifying thrombotic risk
reference.prognosis: Most heterozygous carriers remain asymptomatic throughout life; overall prognosis is favourable, though thrombotic risk increases with homozygosity, additional thrombophilic defects, and transient provoking factors such as hormonal therapy or surgery.
pitfalls: Testing during pregnancy or oestrogen use when acquired activated protein C resistance can confound the functional assay
Extending anticoagulation solely on the basis of a heterozygous result after a provoked event
Advising against all oestrogen exposure without individualised risk assessment
Screening asymptomatic relatives without clear benefit or counselling
management: No treatment and no primary prophylactic anticoagulation for asymptomatic carriers
Standard anticoagulation for an acute venous thromboembolic event, with heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin transitioning to a direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin
Individualised anticoagulation duration, with extended therapy considered for unprovoked, recurrent or homozygous disease
Situational thromboprophylaxis during high-risk periods such as surgery, immobility and the peripartum period
Counselling to avoid oestrogen-containing contraception and hormone replacement therapy, offering alternatives
Modification of additional thrombotic risk factors including obesity, smoking and immobility
Genetic counselling with selective family testing rather than universal screening
